catalog_quote: The rules which determine the position of the stress in Nepali words are complicated. The following guidelines, which should constantly be referred to, apply to the majority of cases. 1. The position of the stress depends upon both the length of the vowels and the nature of the syllables in a given word. ... In general, Nepali words may be stressed on the last syllable, the penultimate (last but one) syllable or the antepenultimate (preceding the last but one) syllable ... In words of two syllables, the stress is on the first (penultimate) syllable when the final syllable is open: ... u-ni, ... khay-ro, sa-dhay ... or if the final syllable is a closed syllable containing a short vowel: ... bha-rat, ... paj-cim ... The stress is on the final syllable, if the final syllable is closed and contains a long vowel: ... pra-cin, cu-rot ... In words of more than two syllables, if the penultimate…

sources.citation: Regmi, Bhim Narayan. 2025. Variation in Nepali Verb Roots: A Phonological Perspective. Gipan 7(1): 121-135. doi:10.3126/gipan.v7i1.84240
sources.note: The article classifies 1892 dictionary verb roots by syllable structure (CV most frequent, then CVC) and explains the 933 roots with variant forms as simplification of underlying super-heavy syllables. It defines syllable weight only for phonotactics and says nothing about word stress, accent or tone; the full text contains no occurrence of stress, accent, tone or pitch.

sources.citation: Chalise, Krishna Prasad. 2024. Sociophonetic Study of Nepali Spoken by the Magar Community in Baglung. Gipan 6(1): 97-105. doi:10.3126/gipan.v6i1.68140
sources.note: The article compares vowel quality, voice quality and consonant changes in the Nepali spoken by Magars in Baglung with standard colloquial Nepali: vowels are more centralized, laryngealized, with F0 about 20-30 Hz lower, and plosives contrast in three places. It says nothing about word stress, accent or tone; the lower F0 is a voice-quality property of all vowels, not a prosodic system.

sources.citation: Singh, Neelam. 2022. F0 Perturbation of Stops in Nepali and Meitei. Nepalese Linguistics 35(1): 137-142. doi:10.3126/nl.v35i01.46571
sources.note: The article measures how the stop consonant changes the pitch of the following vowel in Nepali spoken in Maram (Manipur): voiced aspirated stops lower F0 more than plain voiced stops, and the speakers' level of proficiency in the tonal contact language Meitei made no difference. It says nothing about Nepali word stress and makes no explicit statement about Nepali tone, though it treats Nepali as the non-tonal partner in contact with tonal Meitei, consistent with the catalog's no-tone class.

sources.citation: Roy, Reeny, Susan Dahit & Mingmar. 2019. Acoustic Correlates of Stress in Nepali Language. International Journal of Scientific and Research Publications 9(6): 19-22. DOI 10.29322/IJSRP.9.06.2019.p9005
sources.quote: Measures F0, intensity, duration of 10 disyllabic adjectives read with vs without emphatic stress by 20 speakers; F0 and intensity rise significantly, duration not. States 'There are no reports on the acoustic correlates of stress in Nepali.' No statement on which syllable carries word stress.
sources.venue: International Journal of Scientific and Research Publications
